1 · What you're building & why

ORDER PLAN — alternatives selected 31 October 2026, stock re-checked the same day. The discontinued stack, thermal camera, Pi and goggles were replaced with live listings, and the wrong-band video antenna was replaced with a 5.8 GHz part. The complete order list covers the airframe, analog FPV, payload, tools, configuration laptop and compliance allowance. Merchandise, shown laptop freight and the CA$20 fee allowance total CA$1,714.94; the planning total after 5% GST is CA$1,799.69 before the remaining retailer freight charges. The frame and the flight stack were both out of stock at Rotor Village on that check — confirm at checkout or use the listed alternates.

This build is a 5-inch analog FPV quadcopter carrying a header-equipped Raspberry Pi Zero 2 WH, Pimoroni MLX90640 thermal board and PA1010D GPS. The four-port Qwiic HAT and independent sensor cables let the thermal lens point down while the GPS antenna points up. The selected GEPRC F405 stack supplies regulated 5V/3A for the Pi; the HV video transmitter uses the 4S battery separately.

Software is included: the local payload package provides hotspot grouping, geolocation, GPS/camera integration, append-only logging and an offline coordinate viewer. All 19 synthetic unit tests passed. Physical fit, power stability, detection accuracy and flight behaviour still follow the documented assembly and acceptance tests.

Will this land me a job? The straight answer

No employment outcome is guaranteed. A completed, tested project can be portfolio evidence, but this unbuilt HTML guide is not evidence of a working system, a reference, or interview fluency.

Job Bank groups the data engineer profile under Data scientists (NOC 21211) and rates Alberta prospects Moderate. GoA Systems Analyst is a separate classification; its current Level 1 MRS accepts a related two-year diploma, or a related one-year certificate/qualifying industry certification plus one year of related experience. Experience alone does not satisfy that written education/certification route. The specific job posting and hiring ministry decide relatedness.

Honest next step: finish and test the system before describing it as working. Publish source code, test results, limitations and flight records; then use it as one part of a broader job application rather than a substitute for required education or experience.
What it can and cannot see (the honest capability line)

Design target, not a verified capability: test a controlled warm target from low altitude and record detection rate, false positives and geolocation error. At 30 m AGL, a 55°×35° frame is about 31×20 m, or roughly 1×0.8 m per pixel; a 1 m target may occupy about one pixel and cannot be promised detectable. Day/night, emissivity, atmospheric conditions, motion, tilt and terrain all affect results.

Cannot: replace agency aircraft or declare an area safe. The MLX90640's 32×24 grid is a learning-grade sensor. No detection range, mapping accuracy, professional sensor cost, flight endurance or operational readiness claim is bench-verified for this build.

The one legal line that never bends: no drone may fly over or within 5 nautical miles (9.3 km) of a wildfire below 3,000 ft (CAR 601.15). Real fires are agency airspace — unauthorised drones ground air tankers and endanger crews. You will train on safe heat targets: fire pits, burn barrels, hot plates — on private land, with permission. That is exactly how professionals calibrate their gear too.
Why a drone beats the ground station for your portfolio

An airborne prototype can combine mechanical, radio, sensing, positioning and software work, but it is not inherently more valuable than a tested ground station. FPInnovations' Alberta-funded 2020 report calls the platform only one small part of the solution and says the mission is incomplete until interpreted data reaches the firefighter as a map of GPS-referenced hotspots. That supports the value of integration and reporting, not a hiring guarantee.

What you'll be able to say when it's true
"I built a thermal-camera drone from parts — assembled the airframe, configured the flight controller, wrote and tested the hotspot-detection code, and flew night detection missions over safe targets. At 30 m one pixel covers about 1×0.8 m, so a 1-metre target sits at the edge of what this sensor can resolve — I report the detection rate I actually measured, and every hotspot lands on a map with GPS coordinates. I can explain every part of it. Want to see?"

The demo kit and pitch practice live in the Career tab. Never say any of it until you've measured it.

2 · How it works

One pipeline, six steps. The chain is the same airborne or on the bench — tap any step to see what it does. 1 Sense: the MLX90640 reads 768 temperatures per frame. 2 Detect: the included hotspots.py, backed by 19 passing synthetic tests. 3 Locate: geo.py adds position, altitude and heading. 4 Map: JSONL logging and an offline coordinate viewer. 5 Report: logs keep measured values and limitations. 6 Prove: repeated controlled tests against acceptance targets.

Tap any step above.
📈 Try it — altitude & coverage calculator

Move the sliders to estimate the ideal nadir footprint. This is simple pinhole-camera geometry, not proof of detection performance; the included geo.py implements and tests the ideal-nadir approximation.

Less than two horizontal pixels: a 1 m target may be difficult to distinguish from noise. Detection is not guaranteed; lower the aircraft only where legal and safe, then validate with repeated controlled targets.

Ideal nadir formulas: ground width = 2 × altitude × tan(FOV/2); horizontal metres/pixel = width/32. At 100 m, the 55°×35° lens gives approximately 104.1×63.1 m and 3.25×2.63 m per pixel. Geographic conversion uses ~111,320 m/degree latitude and longitude scaling by cos(latitude), but omits tilt, terrain, lens distortion and GPS/heading/height error.

🔥 What "detecting a fire" actually means

The payload pipeline has three software stages, followed by hardware validation:

  1. Sense: the MLX90640 returns 768 temperatures per frame. A fire is a cluster of hot pixels — say 38 °C background, 300+ °C at the target.
  2. Detect: the included hotspots.py flood-fills edge-connected hot pixels into groups with centroid, size and peak temperature. Synthetic tests cover grouping, thresholds, edges and invalid inputs.
  3. Report: the included geo.py converts pixels using position, altitude and heading; payload.py logs results and map_server.py displays them offline. Detection and coordinate accuracy still require controlled hardware tests.

The same three layers work from the ground, the air, or a satellite feed — that's why the pipeline is the career asset, not the airframe.

⏱ Where & when you may fly (verified TC rules)

Basic operations — what this build flies under (TC page updated 19 Mar 2026):

  • Operating weight no more than 25 kg; measure the completed aircraft rather than relying on the removed 1 kg/3.7 kg estimates. Maintain VLOS.
  • Below 400 ft (122 m) AGL — and no more than 30 m above any building or structure while flying within 61 m of it horizontally. That is CAR 901.25; exceeding it needs a special flight operations certificate. This is the limit beginners break first.
  • More than 30 m horizontally from any person. This is an operations-category boundary, not a universal safe distance.
  • Uncontrolled airspace, more than 5.6 km from the centre of a certified airport, more than 1.9 km from the centre of a heliport; military-aerodrome permission is separate.
  • Register and mark the drone (250 g to 25 kg) and carry proof plus a Pilot Certificate — Basic Operations. The Small Basic exam and registration have fees; age 14+ applies to Basic. The certificate does not expire, but skills must stay current.
Night lighting is necessary, not sufficient (CAR 901.39): the lights must be on and sufficient for the pilot or a visual observer to see the aircraft. A generic LED kit does not by itself make a flight legal; VLOS, airspace, bystander, aerodrome, NOTAM, site and all other applicable rules still apply.
Forest-fire restriction (CAR 601.15): do not operate over a forest-fire area or within 5 nautical miles (9.3 km) of one below 3,000 ft AGL, and do not enter airspace restricted by a NOTAM under 601.16. Check current NOTAMs, Alberta fire bans and local/site rules before flight. Use a hot plate for bench tests; an open test fire also requires landowner permission and every applicable permit.
Edmonton reality check: the 5.6 km airport, 1.9 km heliport and uncontrolled-airspace conditions rule out a lot of the city. Check your intended field with Transport Canada's drone site-selection tool before you drive out — an empty park is not a legal site.

Start this week — Edmonton order plan

Good news about the timing: winter is bench season. Flash the Pi, run the synthetic tests, assemble and inspect indoors, then fly only when weather and site rules allow.

  • Order by retailer: the airframe, radio, FPV and most tools come from Rotor Village in Manitoba; the Pi, thermal board and GPS come from PiShop in Ottawa; the Qwiic HAT/cables come from SparkFun; the laptop and small supplies come from Walmart/Edmonton pickup or delivery. Exact links are in the order document.
  • Freight is separate: Rotor Village and PiShop calculate by weight and destination. SparkFun freight/import charges and any small-Walmart-item charge need checkout quotes. Stock is checked, not reserved.
  • Cold-weather reality (Edmonton winter): LiPos lose punch below −10 °C — keep packs warm in a jacket pocket, expect shorter flights, and never charge a frozen pack. The MLX90640 itself is rated to well below freezing.
  • Compliance first: register the drone ($10) and pass the Transport Canada Small Basic online exam (14+) this week — costs almost nothing and it's the piece that makes every flight after it legal.
Order of operations so nothing stalls: radio first (you can practice on a free simulator like Liftoff while everything else ships), then stack + motors + frame (Weekend 1), then Pi + camera (Weekend 2). The exam and registration can be done tonight.
Buying notes & LiPo safety
  • Soldering: airframe wiring needs it. The payload is solder-free only with a pre-populated Pi header/Qwiic HAT; a standard Zero 2 W needs a header soldered. Budget for a temperature-controlled iron, stand, solder, flux, eye protection, ventilation, cutters, strippers, drivers, meter and smoke stopper — not just a bare iron.
  • LiPo safety: never charge unattended, charge in a LiPo bag, never fly a swollen or damaged pack. This is the one part of the hobby that genuinely bites.
  • The Pi + camera are the payload — if you already ordered them for the old ground-station plan, tick them off.

You will need
  • F405 FC + 50A ESC
  • XT60 battery lead
  • Capacitor
  • Solder + flux + cutters
  • Multimeter
  • Smoke stopper
What to do
  1. Cut each motor wire so it just reaches the ESC.
  2. Tin the pads. Solder the 3 wires from each motor to the ESC.
  3. Solder the XT60 lead and the capacitor — + to +, − to −.
  4. Bolt the flight controller onto the standoffs, above the ESC.

⚠ Safety: glasses on, window open. First power-up goes through the smoke stopper — never direct.

✓ Before you go on
  • Meter confirms polarity · no solder bridges · every wire passes a gentle tug test.

You will need
  • RP1 V2 receiver
  • Phoenix 2 camera
  • Unify HV VTX
  • TBS Triumph PRO 5.8 GHz antenna (SMA)
  • M5F monitor + its 18650 cell
What to do
  1. Wire the receiver: 5V + GND, then receiver TX → the FC's RX pad and receiver RX → the FC's TX pad on a free UART. Read the real pad name off the GEPRC manual — “R2/T2” is unconfirmed for this board.
  2. Clip the receiver's small antenna on before any power.
  3. Wire camera → FC CAM and FC VTX → VTX, so Betaflight's OSD (pack voltage, timer, warnings) reaches your screen — this board has an AT7456E OSD chip. If it turns out to have no analog pads, wire camera → VTX direct and rely on radio telemetry instead.
  4. Mount the VTX and screw the 5.8 GHz antenna on before any power.
  5. In Betaflight enable serial RX + CRSF on that UART. Then flash the RP1 V2 to the same major ExpressLRS version as your Pocket (the receiver ships on v2.4), set the Canada regulatory domain, and only then bind.

⚠ Safety: never power the VTX without its antenna — it burns out in seconds.

✓ Before you go on
  • All radio channels respond · failsafe cuts the throttle · picture on the monitor.

  • LiPo bag
What to do
  1. Put the two 18650 cells in the radio.
  2. Plug the 4S pack into the charger — main plug AND balance lead.
  3. Select LiHV / 4S on the charger screen.
  4. Charge inside the closed LiPo bag and stay next to it the whole time.

⚠ Safety: never charge unattended. Never charge a swollen or damaged pack.

✓ Before you go on
  • Right mode selected · leads undamaged · bag closed beside you.
6

Wire the Pi payload

Soldering iron · the small brain that finds heat

Loading 3D…

The flat picture — the same step drawn on paper. Click it for full size.

You will need
  • Pi Zero 2 WH
  • Qwiic HAT
  • MLX90640 thermal camera
  • PA1010D GPS
  • 2× CAB-17261 female-jumper cables
  • micro-USB pigtail
What to do
  1. Solder the 1×5 headers onto both sensor boards.
  2. Push the Qwiic HAT onto the Pi.
  3. Connect each sensor to the HAT with one cable. The Pimoroni header order is 3V3, SDA, SCL, INT, GND (it maps to Pi pins 1,3,5,7,9), so plug the four cable ends in that order and skip pin 4. Ignore the HAT's silkscreen — SparkFun confirms its SDA/SCL labels are reversed. Trust the cable colours: black GND, red 3V3, blue SDA, yellow SCL.
  4. Power it on the bench. Check both sensors answer: camera 0x33, GPS 0x10.

⚠ Safety: thermal lens points DOWN, GPS antenna points UP. Sensors are 3.3V only — never put 5V on them.

✓ Before you go on
  • Both sensor addresses answer · orientation right · no pin bent backwards.
7

Mount and balance

Hex drivers + zip ties · props still off

You will need
  • Nylon standoffs
  • Zip ties
  • Kevlar strap
  • Battery grip pad
What to do
  1. The rule: the thermal lens needs an unobstructed vertical line to the ground. Mounted on top of the frame it just stares at the top plate and the battery.
  2. Measure before you drill or cut. Hold the Pi and both sensor boards in place and sight down through the lens position. Pi under the bottom plate (or over a cutout you have measured); the MLX90640 hangs below it, lens down; the PA1010D sits on top, patch antenna up.
  3. Fix the Pi on nylon standoffs and zip-tie it down, then add the Kevlar strap as the second lock. Strap the bare MLX breakout — it has no mounting holes of its own.
  4. Route every cable out of the prop circles. Tie the loose ends down.
  5. Slide the battery on the grip pad until the drone balances on its centre.

⚠ Safety: no bare circuit board touches carbon fibre. Nothing loose near spinning props.

✓ Before you go on
  • Lens has a clear view straight down · two holding methods (ties + strap) · balanced centre of gravity · props still off.

You will need

What to do — in this order
  1. Run the software tests and the demo on the laptop.
  2. Power up and wait for a GPS fix.
  3. Check the radio and the video on the bench.
  4. Props OFF — check motor order and direction in Betaflight.
  5. First hover: 1 metre up → land → feel the motors for heat. Never above 122 m (400 ft) AGL.
  6. Heat test: a hot plate among cold things. Write down what it finds.

⚠ Safety: never near a wildfire — the law says 5 nautical miles (9.3 km). Only controlled targets on private land with permission.

✓ Before you go on
  • You have written results before you say “it detects”.

Weekend 1 — build the airframe (tick as you go)
Weekend 2 — build the thermal payload

Payload example — included package, 19 synthetic tests passed

import time, board, busio
import adafruit_mlx90640
from hotspots import find_hotspots   # included tested module in Shad-Drone-Payload

i2c = busio.I2C(board.SCL, board.SDA, frequency=800000)
mlx = adafruit_mlx90640.MLX90640(i2c)
mlx.refresh_rate = adafruit_mlx90640.RefreshRate.REFRESH_2_HZ

frame = [0] * 768
while True:
    try:
        mlx.getFrame(frame)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    for h in find_hotspots(frame, 60, 3):   # threshold 60C, 3+ pixels
        print("HOTSPOT,%.1f,%.1f,%d,%.1f" %
              (h["x"], h["y"], h["pixels"], h["max_c"]))
    time.sleep(0.5)

The MLX90640 uses the documented getFrame API, 768-value buffer and refresh-rate settings at address 0x33. The full GPS/logging/map implementation is in Shad-Drone-Payload. Its 19 synthetic tests and demo passed; physical Pi/sensor integration and airborne accuracy still require the listed acceptance tests.

Weekend 3 — link it up: coordinates on a map
Weekend 4–5 — flight tests over heat targets (the fun part)
Safety first, every time: use a controlled hot plate rather than an open fire. Obtain site permission; check certification, registration, airspace, NOTAMs, weather and fire rules. For Basic operations stay more than 30 m horizontally from any person. These are test acceptance criteria, not pre-existing results.
Weekend 6 — make it undeniable

The pitch, the ask, and the 3-minute demo
"I built a thermal-camera drone from parts — airframe, flight controller, a Raspberry Pi running my own hotspot-detection code. At night, with the lights on like the rules require, it flags a 1-metre heat source at 30 m — right at the edge of the sensor's ~1 m per pixel — and puts it on a map with GPS coordinates, along with the detection rate I measured. I can explain every part of it. Want to see?"

Demo flow (3 min): 0:00 the problem · 0:30 bench: the 768-number frame and the flood fill finding a candle · 1:30 the night flight footage · 2:15 the map marker landing on the target · 2:45 honest limits first: "32×24 sensor, approximate position, prototype — agencies do this with $15k platforms and certified crews. But the pipeline works, and I can explain every line."

Earning a vouch: show don't ask · ask "what would make this useless?" · fix what they say · come back with the fix · then, once they've seen real work: "Would you be comfortable being a reference for me? It's completely fine if not."
